documents: Hilley, Lewicki & Baden (2022), Geophysical Research Letters 49, e2021GL096595, published PDF (10 pages); supporting information not supplied
pages_convention: printed journal pages (n of 10), identical to PDF pages counted from 1; supplementary items cited by their S labels

entry.evidence: A strong seasonality was apparent in the CO2 flux time series

sequences.source_document: Hilley et al. 2022 GRL published PDF

steps.action: The quasi-continuous eddy covariance CO2 flux record at the HSLTK, operating since 2014, is taken from co-author Lewicki's earlier work, which showed seasonal and multiyear changes.
steps.quote: a quasi-continuous time series of CO2 flux was measured by a permanent eddy covariance (Baldocchi, 2003) station at the site

steps.action: The authors ask what processes cause the seasonal and multiyear variations in CO2 flux, so that nonvolcanic signals can be told apart from unrest.
steps.quote: we seek to understand the origins of the seasonal timescale variations in CO2 flux at the HSLTK

steps.action: Three rivals are stated: (a) snow storage or scrubbing of CO2, (b) a seasonal shift in the EC source area (an artifact), and (c) seasonal normal-traction changes on the Mammoth Mountain Fault (fault valving).
steps.quote: Specifically, we seek to test three hypotheses

steps.action: A separate test is designed for each rival: mass-balance and solubility calculations for (a), flux-footprint modelling for (b), and GNSS-derived stresses on the MMF for (c).
steps.quote: Testing each of these hypotheses requires different methodologies, as described below.

steps.action: The EC series is filtered (Mauder & Foken quality flags, friction velocity >0.3 m/s, iterative Z-score outlier rejection), then a daily, yearly and error-function multiyear model is fitted by Nelder-Mead, giving the amplitudes and a 1,111 g m-2 d-1 drop centred on 3 March 2017.
steps.quote: The measured EC CO2 flux time series shows semi-diurnal, diurnal, and yearly amplitudes of 176, 123, and 496 g

steps.action: A mass balance using the maximum snow depth of 1.6 m and an upper-bound porosity of 0.85 shows that the seasonal flux deficit would fill the snowpack with CO2 in 1.9 days.
steps.quote: the entire observed seasonal snow depth would fill with CO2 in 1.9 days

steps.action: Storage of CO2 in the snowpack is rejected as the cause of the wintertime flux suppression.
steps.quote: [...] in snow cannot account for the suppression of wintertime CO2 fluxes

steps.action: From CO2 solubility, the infiltration rate needed for scrubbing is computed (0.42 m/d) and set against the cited annual precipitation of 1.0-1.5 m/yr.
steps.quote: requires a daily water infiltration rate of 0.42 m d−1

steps.action: Scrubbing of CO2 by infiltrating snowmelt and rain is rejected as the cause of the seasonality.
steps.quote: Scrubbing of CO2 is not a viable mechanism to explain the seasonality of CO2 fluxes at the HSLTK

steps.action: The Flux Footprint Prediction model is driven by measured meteorology and a snow-corrected measurement height and applied to the June 2015 soil-flux map, giving the EC series that the artifact rival predicts for June 2015 to May 2016.
steps.quote: we modeled an EC CO2 flux time series from 1 June 2015 to 31 May 2016 based on a changing flux source weight function

steps.action: The modelled and measured seasonal signals are compared: the model gives about half the amplitude and lags the measurements by 162 days.
steps.quote: the changing flux source area can explain only about half of the measured seasonal amplitude variations in CO2 flux

steps.action: The rival that the seasonality is an artifact of the EC source area is rejected.
steps.quote: Thus, changes in the EC flux source area cannot explain the observed seasonal variations in CO2 flux.

steps.action: Daily GNSS position solutions from the regional continuous network (UNAVCO) are obtained, then detrended, cleaned of outliers and Gaussian-smoothed with a 10-day timescale.
steps.quote: we use daily solutions for continuously operating GNSS stations in the area (Table S1)

steps.action: Transient strains are computed with a modified Strain2D and GPSGridder interpolation (Poisson's ratio 0.3), converted to plane-stress elastic stresses and resolved as normal tractions on the vertical MMF.
steps.quote: we used the GNSS network to calculate the seasonal normal stress changes acting along the MMF (Movie S1), assuming stresses are elastic

steps.action: The inferred normal tractions are compared with the 10-day-smoothed CO2 flux; less compressive stress goes with higher flux, with R2 = 0.58, and the stress becomes more compressive after the 2017 swarms.
steps.quote: with higher measured CO2 fluxes corresponding to less compressive normal stresses acting along the MMF

steps.action: The relation is rechecked with strains from unsmoothed GNSS data (Figure S2) and after removing the multiyear trends from both series (R2 = 0.25, Figure S1).
steps.quote: [...] trend is observed when using strains derived from the unsmoothed GNSS observations

steps.action: Fault valving by seasonal, regional-scale stress changes is kept as a viable explanation of the seasonality.
steps.quote: fault valving that is controlled by seasonal, regional-scale stress changes provides a viable explanation

steps.action: Drawing on cited studies of hydrologic loading, poroelastic infiltration and drought cycles, the claim is refined: regional rather than local hydrology modulates the flux, indirectly, through solid-earth stresses, including the multiyear 2017 change.
steps.quote: regional hydrology may play an important role by modulating elastic stresses in the crust through several distinct pathways

steps.action: Rearranging the solubility relation bounds scrubbing at about 7 g m-2 d-1 per metre of annual infiltration; set against cited mean fluxes of volcanic systems, scrubbing is rejected as a general modulator.
steps.quote: Snowmelt scrubbing of CO2 is therefore unlikely to appreciably reduce annual volcanic CO2 emissions

tree.answer: Seasonal and multiyear (2017) variations in volcanic CO2 flux at the HSLTK, inherited from earlier EC monitoring
Flux is observed directly by EC; stress on the fault is not, and is inferred from GNSS strains
Explain the origin of the variations so that nonvolcanic signals can be separated from unrest
Three rivals: snow storage or scrubbing, EC footprint artifact, fault valving
Yes: snow fill time, required infiltration, and footprint amplitude and phase computed for the rivals
Conditions found: natural hydrologic seasons, the 2017 drought end and swarms

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Nature repeats the seasonal cycle about six times (2014-2020)
Survives unsmoothed GNSS and multiyear detrending, with a weaker R2 of 0.25
Snow and footprint rivals excluded; fault valving kept as a viable explanation

end.claim: Seasonal and multiyear changes in CO2 flux at the HSLTK are best explained by fault valving, as GNSS-inferred normal-traction changes on the Mammoth Mountain Fault open and close the gas conduit; snow storage, scrubbing and EC footprint artifacts are excluded.

decisive_move.sentence: Without inferring the time series of normal tractions on the MMF from the GNSS network, there would be no positive evidence for fault valving, only the exclusion of the other two rivals.

gates.evidence: Both the EC and GNSS data came from existing monitoring (Lewicki 2021a,b; UNAVCO), not acquired under the hypotheses. The snow and footprint rivals faced calculations they could have passed and failed them. The fault-valving correlation could have failed (wrong sign, no correlation), but no threshold was set in advance, and the detrended R2 falls to 0.25. Nothing is stated as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Nelder-Mead simplex algorithm with adaptive parameters (Gao & Han 2012)
iterative Z-score outlier rejection with an erf-based maximum expected Z
solubility of CO2 in water at low pressure (Carroll et al. 1991)

novelty_claims.quote: With this information, new and unexpected signals have been observed at Mammoth Mountain, California

limits: No review file was supplied; the acknowledgments name reviewers, but what they changed is unknown. The supporting information (Figures S1-S2, Tables S1-S2, Movie S1) was not supplied, so the V checks rest on the main text's description. The R2 of 0.58 includes the multiyear trend shared by both series; once detrended, R2 falls to 0.25, so the seasonal sub-claim is weaker than the headline. Other nonvolcanic drivers cited in the introduction (barometric pressure, soil moisture, temperature, wind) are not stated as rivals. The footprint test covers one year, duplicated, and one soil-flux map. Surface stresses are assumed to represent stresses at depth, and plane stress is assumed. Sub-claim statuses: the curve-fit amplitudes are estimates, reported without uncertainties except the residual standard deviation (estimate_with_resolution, weak); linking the multiyear 2017 change to the swarms, drought and climate is best_explanation at a lower level ('plausible'); the exclusions of snow storage, scrubbing and the footprint artifact are excluded. Composition: natures_repetition was chosen because the positive evidence is a correlation across naturally repeated seasonal cycles, but the walk also eliminates rivals as a trace series does, and the claim is a best explanation. Inference: coding the general scrubbing bound (p. 7) as a generalization check is generous, since it compares a calculation with cited flux magnitudes rather than new data.

disagreements.target: Snowmelt and rainfall scrubbing of CO2 as a modulator of tree-kill soil CO2 (McGee & Gerlach, 1998)
disagreements.support: Solubility calculations show that the required infiltration would use up the annual precipitation in 2-4 days, and that scrubbing can remove at most about 7 g m-2 d-1 per metre of water.
disagreements.quote: Snowmelt scrubbing of CO2 is therefore unlikely to appreciably reduce annual volcanic CO2 emissions

disagreements.target: Attribution of volcanic CO2 flux variations to local nonvolcanic or environmental factors (Granieri et al. 2003; Rogie et al. 2001; [...]
disagreements.support: The local snow, scrubbing and footprint mechanisms are excluded quantitatively, and regional stress changes from GNSS match the flux.
disagreements.quote: Our work shows that local seasonal hydrology at the HSLTK may not play a primary role in modulating CO2 fluxes

alternatives_considered.chosen: Fault valving by normal-traction changes on the MMF
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Snow storage or scrubbing; seasonal EC source-area artifact
alternatives_considered.reason: The storage, scrubbing and footprint calculations fail to match the observed amplitude and phase

alternatives_considered.chosen: GNSS displacements smoothed with a 10-day Gaussian
alternatives_considered.reason: Matching the GNSS observations; the unsmoothed run checks that the relation is resolved above the noise

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Multiyear decreases subtracted from flux and stress (R2 = 0.25)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Plane-stress conditions with stresses resolved on a vertical MMF
alternatives_considered.reason: The MMF appears vertical from its outcrop pattern, and plane stress is consistent with GPSGridder's assumptions
